title: Lower Bounded Wildcards (? super T) & Contravariance
summary: Master <? super T>: writing elements of type T safely into consumer collections, and contravariance in flexible API design.
prerequisites: Upper Bounded Wildcards (? extends T) & Covariance
learningObjectives: Master the lower bounded wildcard syntax: List<? super T>
Understand contravariance: inverting the subtyping hierarchy for consumer collections
Analyze why writing elements of type T to a <? super T> collection is 100% type-safe
Recognize the reading limitation: elements read from <? super T> can only be typed as Object
expectedOutcomes: Ability to design flexible consumer sinks and data populators using contravariant generics
Mastery of the 'C' (Consumer) in the PECS architectural principle

activities.title: Practical Context: Standard Electronic Recycling Disposal Chutes

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Standard Electronic Recycling Disposal Chutes
analogy.story:
Imagine a recycling center with a chute designated for disposing of obsolete smartphones: `DisposalChute<? super Smartphone>`. The chute could lead to a bin strictly for smartphones, a larger container for portable electronics, or a massive industrial crusher for all solid consumer goods.

No matter which of those three bins is attached below, you can safely drop your smartphone down the chute. Because a smartphone is an electronic device, and also a physical solid good, it is completely compatible with any of those bins (safe write).

However, if you reach your hand blindly into the bottom of that chute to pull out an item, you have no guarantee what you will pull out: it might be a toaster, a microwave, or a laptop. The only thing you can be certain of is that it is a physical Object (read yields Object).
analogy.keyTakeaway: Lower bounded wildcards (? super T) make collections safe consumers (sinks). You can safely insert elements of type T, but reading only yields Object.

activities.title: Contravariance with <? super T>: Safe Insertion & Object Bounds

keyTakeaways: Lower bounded wildcards (? super T) introduce contravariance to Java generics
List<? super Integer> accepts List<Integer>, List<Number>, and List<Object>
Writing elements of type T (or any subtype of T) into List<? super T> is 100% type-safe
Reading from List<? super T> only guarantees the return type is java.lang.Object
This is the 'C' (Consumer) in the PECS principle: Consumer Super

activities.content:
### What Is Contravariance?

A type system is **contravariant** if it inverts the subtyping relationship: if `Sub` is a subtype of `Super`, then `Consumer<Super>` is treated as a subtype of `Consumer<Sub>`.

In Java, **lower bounded wildcards (`<? super T>`)** introduce contravariance to generic method parameters. A parameter `List<? super Integer>` can accept:
* `List<Integer>`
* `List<Number>`
* `List<Object>`

---

### Why Insertion into `<? super T>` Is Always Type-Safe

When a method accepts `List<? super Integer>`, what is the most specific type the underlying list could be? It could be `List<Integer>`, or a broader supertype like `List<Number>` or `List<Object>`.

```java
public static void addNumbers(List<? super Integer> consumer) {
    consumer.add(Integer.valueOf(10)); // 100% COMPILE SAFE!
    consumer.add(Integer.valueOf(20)); // 100% COMPILE SAFE!
}
```
Because `Integer` is compatible with `Integer`, and `Integer` is a valid `Number`, and `Integer` is a valid `Object`, **no matter what concrete collection was passed in, inserting an `Integer` can never corrupt the underlying list!**

---

### The Read Restriction on `<? super T>`

Conversely, what happens if you attempt to read an element from `List<? super Integer>`?
```java
List<? super Integer> list = ...;
// Integer x = list.get(0); // COMPILE ERROR!
// Number n = list.get(0);  // COMPILE ERROR!
Object obj = list.get(0);   // ALLOWED: The ONLY safe read!
```
Because the list might actually be `List<Object>`, the compiler has no guarantee that the element stored at index 0 is an `Integer` or even a `Number`. Therefore, all reads from a `<? super T>` collection are typed strictly as **`java.lang.Object`**.

---

### The Consumer Contract: Data Destination Sink

Whenever a method's job is to write data into a collection (the collection consumes elements), always use `<? super T>`:
```java
public static void populateEvens(int count, List<? super Integer> destination) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        destination.add(i * 2);
    }
}
```
This allows callers to pass a `List<Integer>`, a `List<Number>`, or a `List<Object>` into `populateEvens` seamlessly.

---

### Executable Demonstration: Flexible Consumer Sink

questions.question: Which of the following method invocations will compile if the method signature is 'void sink(List<? super Integer> list)'?
questions.explanation: <? super Integer> specifies an unknown type that is a supertype of Integer. Since Number is a direct superclass of Integer, ArrayList<Number> is assignable to List<? super Integer>. Double and Float are siblings, not supertypes.

questions.question: What is the return type when invoking list.get(0) on a collection declared as 'List<? super String>'?
options: It triggers a compile error because get() cannot be called at all
questions.explanation: Because List<? super String> could point to a List<Object>, the compiler has no guarantee of any specific subtype. The only type that all possible bounds share in common is java.lang.Object.

activities.title: Senior Engineer Interview: Why Lower Bounds Are Prohibited on Class Declarations

qaList.question: Why does Java support lower bounds on wildcards ('<? super T>') but strictly forbids lower bounds on class and method type parameter declarations ('<T super Integer>')?
qaList.answer: Lower bounded type parameters ('<T super Integer>') are semantically meaningless and redundant for classes and methods. An upper bound like '<T extends Number>' restricts T to a specific subtree of the class hierarchy, allowing you to invoke methods of Number (like doubleValue()). However, a lower bound like '<T super Integer>' would mean T could be Integer, Number, or Object. Because the only methods common to all supertypes of Integer are the methods of Object, declaring '<T super Integer>' gives the compiler no extra method capabilities beyond plain Object. On wildcards, however, '<? super T>' is critical because it tells the compiler which objects can be safely PASSED AS ARGUMENTS into methods like list.add(T), enabling safe contravariant writing.

practiceProblems.title: Contravariant Natural Number Generator
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a method fillSequence(List<? super Integer> sink, int n) that adds integers from 1 up to n (inclusive) into the provided sink list.

practiceProblems.title: Transfer Elements from Producer to Consumer
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a generic method transferAll(List<? extends T> producer, List<? super T> consumer) that copies all elements from producer to consumer using the PECS principle.

practiceProblems.title: Filter Evens into Consumer Sink
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a method copyEvens(List<Integer> source, List<? super Integer> sink) that copies all even integers from source into sink.

practiceProblems.title: Contravariant Safe Ingestion If Absent
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a method addIfAbsent(List<? super String> sink, List<?> existing, String item) that adds item to sink only if item does not exist in the existing list.

practiceProblems.title: Contravariant Element Replicator
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a method replicate(List<? super T> sink, T element, int count) that appends element into sink count times.
